newsitem.title: CUBA: Cuba says Peru rebels could get asylum.
newsitem.headline: Cuba says Peru rebels could get asylum.

text.p: Cuba confirmed on Thursday it had accepted a formal Japanese request to grant asylum to Peruvian Marxist rebels holding 72 hostages at the Japanese ambassador's home in Lima if there is a negotiated settlement to the 93-day crisis.
Japanese Vice Foreign Minister Masahiko Komura delivered the request to President Fidel Castro in Havana on Wednesday evening.

Komura, who arrived in Cuba after two days talks with the government in Lima, left on Thursday afternoon for the Dominican Republic, which is also believed to have offered to take in some of the hostage-takers.
Cuba made the asylum offer earlier this month, making clear all parties involved in the hostage crisis, including the rebels, would have to be in formal agreement.
The hostage-takers have so far reserved comment on the possibility of asylum in Cuba.
Cuba's comment on Thursday on Komura's visit was brief and carefully worded.

"Komura carries an official request from the Japanese government for Cuba to receive, for humanitarian reasons, the Tupac Amaru Revolutionary Movement (MRTA) group that are occupying the Japanese embasy in Lima," the ruling Communist Party newspaper Granma said.
"The Cuban government ratified its willingess to cooperate where possible in the solution to the situation, on the basis of an agreement between the involved parties," it added.

Asked about the Cuban offer, Cuba's deputy foreign minister Jorge Bolanos noted a solution still depended on negotiations in Lima. He was speaking to reporters at Havana airport after seeing Komura off.
Asked about speculation that Japan might pay Cuba in return for taking in the hostage-takers, Bolanos said: "The only interest that moves Cuba is humanitarian."
Japanese government sources speaking earlier on Thursday in Tokyo also said Castro had underlined that Cuba viewed its offer as a humanitarian gesture.
"Our acceptance on this issue is from a humanitarian point of view. Cuba is not a country to take in terrorism," the sources quoted Castro as saying.

Castro earlier this month told Peru's President Alberto Fujimori that Cuba was willing to take in the hostage-takers, saying Havana viewed this as a "moral duty" but adding the solution could only be found if all parties involved agreed.

While the MRTA are said to be inspired by Cuba's revolution, Havana for weeks declined comment on the affair, saying only that it wanted to see a peaceful solution. And Castro's government waited to be asked by Fujimori before offering possible asylum to the rebels.

Despite Japan's efforts to push the crisis toward a negotiated settlement, the MRTA guerrillas have not indicated they will accept asylum or end the siege for anything less than the release of their jailed comrades, their key demand.
In Lima on Thursday, Fujimori vehemently denied reports that his government would free jailed MRTA members to end the crisis.
But if the rebels do eventually come to Cuba, there will be precedents.
Castro mediated in June 1995 to secure the freedom of the brother of former Colombian president Cesar Gaviria. Some of the kidnappers and their families flew to Cuba.
Havana also intervened to help resolve a crisis in Colombia in 1980 when guerrillas of the M-19 movement seized 14 ambassadors at the Dominican Embassy residence in Bogota.
